name: Water loading / hydration maxxing

lead: Water loading, or hydration maxxing, is drinking large volumes of water to get fuller, clearer-looking skin and a less puffy face. It is a common fixture of skincare and depuffing routines.

Users say good hydration plumps the skin and helps flush retained water from the face. Reference sources describe the 'eight glasses a day' advice as unscientific and say thirst is a better guide to how much to drink; US and EU intake guidelines for total water, including food, run from about 2.0 to 4.0 L a day depending on sex and body.

paras: People carry a bottle and spread intake through the day, often adding more in the morning or before a photo or event. It is usually paired with other skin and depuffing habits such as sleep, lower salt intake and skincare. Users describe skin and puffiness changes over days to weeks.

Drinking too much water too quickly can cause hyponatremia, a dangerous drop in blood sodium that reference sources say can cause death within minutes to hours. Thirst is the usual guide to intake, and people with kidney, heart or other conditions that affect fluid balance should be especially careful.

web.title: Europe PMC records for water intake and skin studies

angle.text: Users drink large amounts of water to plump the skin and reduce facial puffiness, making the face look fuller and clearer. It is a common part of skincare and depuffing routines. Fixed targets such as eight glasses are not backed by research, and the skin effect is reported mainly by users.

lead: Water loading, sometimes called hydration maxxing, is the practice of deliberately drinking large quantities of water, with the aim of plumper, clearer-looking skin and less facial puffiness. It is one of the most common wellness habits in appearance communities because it is free, easy and tied to a widely held belief that well-hydrated skin looks better.

Guideline figures give a sense of ordinary intake. The US Adequate Intake for total water, counting water from food, is 4.0 L a day for men and 3.0 L for women, while the European Food Safety Authority recommends 2.5 L for men and 2.0 L for women; about 80 percent of total intake comes from drink [1]. Wikipedia describes the "eight glasses a day" rule as not scientifically based and says thirst is a better guide [1].

Two small studies have looked at water intake and skin. A 2015 study of 49 healthy women reported that about 2 L of extra water a day for a month changed superficial and deep skin hydration, mostly in women who habitually drank less [2]. A 2024 study of 43 women found that moisturizer use had a more favourable effect on skin hydration than extra water [2]. Drinking far more than the body needs can cause water intoxication and hyponatremia, a potentially fatal drop in blood sodium [1][3].

paras: Needs vary with activity, age, health and environment, and about 80 percent of total water intake comes from drink, with the remainder from food [1]. Wikipedia notes that the common eight-glasses advice lacks a scientific basis and that thirst is a better guide than a fixed amount [1].

In a 2015 study in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology, Palma and colleagues grouped 49 healthy women by habitual intake, with the cut-off at 3,200 mL a day. Roughly 2 L of additional water daily for one month significantly changed superficial and deep skin hydration, especially in the lower-intake group, and biomechanical measures shifted similarly. The authors concluded that higher dietary water may positively affect skin physiology, particularly in people who drink little [2].

In a 2024 Annals of Dermatology study of 43 healthy women, people who drank more than 1 L daily were compared with those who drank less. Some forearm, hand and shin sites in groups receiving added water or moisturizer showed higher skin hydration at week 4 than at baseline, and moisturizer had the more favourable effect [2].

A 2023 cross-sectional study of acne patients in Karachi found that lower daily water intake (fewer than eight glasses) was significantly associated with acne, alongside oily and sugary foods [2]. No studies were found on high water intake and facial puffiness.

Water intoxication is a potentially fatal disturbance of brain function that occurs when excess water intake pushes electrolytes out of safe limits. Wikipedia lists water-drinking contests and prolonged exercise with heavy fluid intake as causes behind most deaths in healthy people; early symptoms include headache, confusion and irritability, and severe cases cause brain swelling, seizures, coma and death [3].

Healthy kidneys can excrete roughly 800 mL to 1 L of water per hour, and drinking six litres in three hours has caused a death [3]. Documented cases include a 2007 radio contest in which a woman died after drinking nearly 2 US gallons [3].
